lead: HVDC transmission sends bulk power as direct current between two converter stations. At one end a rectifier turns AC into DC, the line carries DC with only a small ripple, and at the other end an inverter turns it back into AC. With no charging current and no reactive voltage drop, DC wins on very long overhead routes, on undersea cables and between grids that are not synchronised. Power flow is set by converter control, not by the angle between two AC systems. Links run between regions and from offshore wind farms to shore.
prereq: You need: three-phase controlled rectifiers, inversion mode and the effect of source inductance (controlled rectifiers), PWM bridges with IGBTs (DC-AC inverters), and thyristor and IGBT ratings (power semiconductor devices).

blocks.text: An AC line has series inductance and shunt capacitance. On a long line the capacitance draws charging current, so part of the conductor current carries no useful power and the receiving-end voltage rises at light load. An AC submarine cable is worse: its capacitance is large and the whole length carries charging current, so AC sea crossings are limited to a few tens of kilometres.

A DC line carries only load current; the loss is I²R. For the same power DC needs two conductors instead of three, or one conductor with an earth return, so the cost per kilometre falls. Beyond a break-even distance, hundreds of kilometres for overhead lines, DC costs less overall even though the terminal stations cost more.

DC also separates the two grids. Rectifier and inverter need not stay in step, so a link joins systems of different frequency or systems not synchronised at all. Some back-to-back HVDC stations do this inside one country. Power flow is set by converter control, not by the angle between two voltage phasors, so it can be held at any value and reversed in a fraction of a second.

The classic station uses thyristors in a 12-pulse bridge, two of the three-phase controlled rectifiers met earlier in the subject. A thyristor turns on by gate pulse but turns off only when its current falls to zero, so the AC line voltage itself must push current from one valve to the next. This is line commutation, and it means the station must sit on a strong AC network.

items: Converter transformer: star-star and star-delta secondaries, giving the 30° shift and the insulation against DC.
Two 6-pulse bridges 30° apart make one 12-pulse converter: the 5th and 7th AC-side harmonics cancel, so the lowest AC-side harmonic is the 11th and the DC ripple is at the 12th and 24th.
AC filters: tuned branches for the 11th, 13th and higher, plus a high-pass branch; they also supply part of the reactive power.
Smoothing reactor: a series inductor in the DC line that keeps the DC current continuous at light load and slows the rise of fault current.
Ground electrode or metallic return, and surge arresters across valves and transformers.

blocks.text: Reactive power: a line-commutated bridge absorbs reactive power at both ends. A working figure is Q ≈ 0.5 P<sub>d</sub>, about half the DC power, at the rectifier and at the inverter. Filters and capacitors supply part of it and synchronous condensers the rest, so a weak AC system cannot feed a line-commutated station.

Commutation failure: the inverter valve that is turning off must be given time, the extinction angle γ, to regain its blocking ability. A dip in AC voltage or a jump in DC current steals that time, the current fails to transfer, and the bridge briefly short-circuits the DC terminal so that DC voltage collapses. The link recovers within a few cycles once AC voltage returns, so one event is not a permanent trip.

A voltage-source converter station uses IGBT bridges with PWM, like the inverters of the DC-AC inverters topic. An IGBT turns off on command, so the bridge does not need the AC line to commutate. It can therefore feed a passive network and black-start a dead grid after a blackout, work into a weak grid, and control active and reactive power independently. It reverses power by reversing the DC current while keeping the DC voltage polarity fixed, which suits extruded cable insulation. Losses are a little higher than for LCC and station ratings were traditionally smaller, but VSC dominates new cable links.

P<sub>d</sub> is the total DC power in watts; V<sub>d</sub> is the DC voltage in volts and I<sub>d</sub> the line current in amperes. For a bipolar link V<sub>d</sub> is the pole-to-pole voltage, twice the pole-to-ground value, and I<sub>d</sub> is the current in one pole, so P<sub>d</sub> = (2 × pole-to-ground voltage) × pole current. For a monopolar link V<sub>d</sub> is the pole-to-ground voltage and I<sub>d</sub> the conductor current, and the same product still holds.

Arrangements. Monopolar: one conductor, with return through earth or through a metallic return conductor. Bipolar: two poles, one at +V<sub>d</sub>/2 and one at −V<sub>d</sub>/2 to earth, each carrying half the power, and in balanced operation the earth current is nearly zero. If a pole trips, the healthy pole keeps running in monopolar mode with ground return, so half the power stays on. The ground electrode must have low resistance and is sited carefully for environmental reasons. A DC network with more than two stations is called MTDC.

spec.aria: Rectifier and inverter stations, each with a plus and a minus pole converter, joined by two DC lines with smoothing reactors; the station midpoints are earthed.

examples.question: A ±500 kV bipolar HVDC link transmits 2000 MW. Find (a) the DC current in each pole, (b) the power still delivered if one pole trips and the return is through ground, and (c) the reactive power each line-commutated station draws at 50% of DC power.
steps: The link is bipolar at ±500 kV, so the pole-to-pole DC voltage is V<sub>d</sub> = 2 × 500 kV = 1000 kV = 1000 × 10³ V.
Total DC power is P<sub>d</sub> = 2000 MW = 2000 × 10⁶ W, and P<sub>d</sub> = V<sub>d</sub> × I<sub>d</sub>.
So I<sub>d</sub> = 2000 × 10⁶ / (1000 × 10³) = 2000 A in each pole. Check: each pole carries 500 kV × 2000 A = 1000 MW, and two poles give 2000 MW.
With one pole out, the remaining pole runs at 500 kV to ground and carries the same 2000 A: P = 500 × 10³ × 2000 = 1000 × 10⁶ W = 1000 MW.
At 50% of DC power the DC power is only 1000 MW, so each station draws Q ≈ 0.5 × 1000 MW = 500 MVAr. At the full 2000 MW each station would draw about 1000 MVAr.
examples.answer: The pole current is 2000 A, the link still delivers 1000 MW in monopolar ground-return operation, and at 50% power each station draws about 500 MVAr (about 1000 MVAr each at full power).
examples.check:
V_pp = 1000e3
P_total = 2000e6
I_d = P_total / V_pp
V_pole = V_pp / 2
P_mono = V_pole * I_d
Q_station = 0.5 * 0.5 * P_total / 1e6
print(I_d)
print(P_mono / 1e6)
print(Q_station)

traps: Putting the pole-to-ground voltage into P<sub>d</sub> = V<sub>d</sub> I<sub>d</sub> for a bipolar link. The formula uses the pole-to-pole voltage, twice the pole-to-ground value, with the current of one pole.
Assuming the inverter generates reactive power while the rectifier absorbs it. Both line-commutated stations absorb reactive power, roughly half the DC power each; the filters only supply part of it.
Treating a commutation failure as a permanent fault. It is a temporary short circuit across the DC terminal, and the link recovers within a few cycles after the AC voltage returns.
Swapping the reversal mechanisms: an LCC reverses DC voltage polarity at constant current direction, while a VSC reverses current direction at constant voltage polarity.
Believing an HVDC line has charging current or a reactive voltage drop. It has neither, and that is exactly why DC suits long overhead routes and cables.

quiz.q: What is the lowest-order harmonic on the AC side of a 12-pulse converter?
quiz.a: The 11th. The 5th and 7th cancel between the two 6-pulse bridges that are 30° apart.

quiz.q: State the role of the smoothing reactor in an HVDC station.
quiz.a: It is a series inductor in the DC line. It smooths the DC current, keeps it continuous at light load, and limits the rate of rise of fault current.

quiz.q: Why can a line-commutated station not feed a network that has no generation of its own?
quiz.a: Thyristors turn off only when their current falls to zero, so the AC line voltage must drive commutation. A dead network has no voltage, so there is nothing to commutate against; the station needs a live AC source.

quiz.q: A ±600 kV bipolar link delivers 3000 MW. Find the pole current and the power left if one pole trips with ground return.
Both stations of an LCC link absorb reactive power. Why does this not break energy balance?
quiz.a: Reactive power is not real energy; it swings between the AC system and the converter twice per cycle. It shifts the AC current away from the voltage phase, raising line current and loss, and must be supplied locally by filters, capacitors or synchronous condensers.

quiz.q: Why is DC the usual choice for a 200 km submarine crossing but not always for a 200 km overhead line?
quiz.a: In a cable the large capacitance draws charging current over the whole length, so AC cables are limited to a few tens of kilometres; a DC cable has no charging current. For an overhead line the DC advantage exists too, but two converter stations cost a lot, so the break-even distance is hundreds of kilometres.

quiz.q: Why does a VSC station reverse power by reversing the DC current instead of the voltage polarity?
quiz.a: Fixed polarity keeps the insulation stress in one direction, which suits extruded cables, and the current controller can reverse the current directly without re-arranging the DC circuit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most large new HVDC stations are now modular multilevel converters, a VSC built from many series half-bridges that switch in small steps, giving low harmonics with no large filter banks at the cost of many submodules and complex control. Multi-terminal DC grids, where several stations share one DC network, are the active research area for collecting offshore wind. Hybrid links put an LCC at one end and a VSC at the other. Wide band-gap devices such as SiC are being tried inside submodules to cut losses. Search next for modular multilevel converter, VSC-HVDC and HVDC grid.
